doc_name: List of prime ministers of Nepal
text: The position of the Prime Minister of Nepal (Nepali: नेपालको प्रधानमन्त्री, romanized: Nepālko Pradhānmantrī) has evolved through various names and structures throughout Nepalese history. In the early period of the Shah dynasty, the Mulkajis (Chief Kajis) or Chautariyas served as prime ministers within a council consisting of 4 Chautariyas, 4 Kajis, and other officers known as Bharadars, who were typically drawn from high-caste and politically influential families such as the Pande, Basnyat, and Thapa families. The nobility of Gorkha, primarily composed of Chhetri families, played a significant role in civil administration. In 1804, Rana Bahadur Shah established a single authoritative position called Mukhtiyar, which held executive powers of the nation. This position remained the head of the executive until November 1843, when Mathabar Singh Thapa was appointed as Mukhtiyar and Prime Minister and also became the Chief of the Nepalese Army. During the Rana dynasty, the prime ministerial office became hereditary, and officeholders were granted additional titles, including Maharaja of Lamjang and Kaski, Supreme Commander-in-Chief of Nepal, and Grand Master of the Royal Orders of Nepal. After the 1951 revolution, non-aristocratic individuals such as Matrika Prasad Koirala held the office under the authority of the King. The first general election was held in 1959, resulting in Bishweshwar Prasad Koirala becoming the first elected prime minister. However, he was removed and imprisoned in the 1960 coup d'état led by King Mahendra, who established the Panchayat system, a regime without democratic governance, until 1990. The Jana Andolan movement in 1990 led to the transformation of the Kingdom into a constitutional monarchy. This was later disrupted by the 2005 coup d'état by King Gyanendra. Following the Loktantra Andolan movement in 2006, the monarchy was abolished on 28 May 2008 by the 1st Constituent Assembly, and Nepal was declared a federal parliamentary republic. The current constitution was adopted on 20 September 2015, with KP Sharma Oli becoming the first prime minister under this constitution. All prime ministers of Nepal from 1768 to 1950 were Chhetris, except for Ranga Nath Poudyal, who was a Khas Brahmin. Among the 23 men elected since Nepal gained democracy after the Rana dynasty in 1951, 15 were Khas Brahmins, 3 were Thakuri, 2 were Newar Shresthas, 2 were Chhetri, and 1 was a Sanyasi/Dasnami. Executive power was historically shared between the Kajis and Chautariyas.
